headline: Nine Hours to Atlantis, Two Slot Bluefin, and a Wahoo We Never Saw Coming
subhead: The run's still long and the fuel math still matters, but the canyon edges east of Montauk are finally paying for the trip.
body_markdown:
We left the dock at Montauk at 0300 Tuesday, and by the time the loran numbers matched the chart plotter's guess at the Atlantis edge, we'd burned through a third of a tank and most of the coffee. That's the math out here — call it four hours running at twenty-two knots to cover the ninety-some miles, and that's if the swell cooperates. It didn't complain much this week. Three-to-four foot period swell out of the south, nothing that put anybody on the rail wishing they'd stayed home, but enough to remind you why you fuel heavy and never trust the gauge on the way back.

We found the temperature break we wanted about a mile inside where the chart said it should be — cooler shelf water running 69 degrees butting up against warmer canyon water pushing into the mid-70s. That's the kind of seam that holds bait, and where there's bait on the Atlantis wall this time of July, there's tuna working it. We set up a chunk line on the down-current side, butterfish and a handful of menhaden, 6/0 circle hooks on 60-pound fluoro, and let it soak with the current instead of against it. Took about forty minutes before the first rod bent — a bluefin right in that 27-to-under-47-inch slot everybody's fishing for since the trophy category closed on the third. Second fish came an hour later, same size class, same story. Two-fish limit filled by 0800, which on a long run like this is about as good a morning as you can ask the ocean for.

What we didn't boat was the wahoo that hit a high-speed lure on the way to the chunk spot — ran the drag down hard for maybe ten seconds and then came unbuttoned on a jump we only half saw. That's wahoo fishing for you out here; you get a look and a story, not always a fish in the box. If you want a better crack at them, the morning bite window right at first light on the edge, trolling deep-diving plugs or wahoo bombs at 10 to 12 knots along the drop where the bottom falls from 600 to 1,200 fathoms, is when they show. We'll try again next trip.

The bigger picture this week backs up what the boats running to Veatch and Hydrographer have been reporting — stable high pressure has held for the better part of ten days now, and that kind of weather window is rare enough out here that you fish it hard while it lasts. Warm eddy water has pushed in tight to the canyon edges, and it's dragging yellowfin and a scattering of bigeye up onto the troll. Standard spread — Ilanders and naked ballyhoo, cedar plugs off the shortest rigger, green machines out the back — worked at 6 to 7 knots along the 68-to-72-degree break has been putting fish in the boat at Hydrographer, with reports of similar action pushing east toward Oceanographer. Mahi have been mixed in wherever the boats find floating structure or a stray lobster buoy — nothing to build a trip around by itself, but a welcome bonus when the tuna bite slows midday.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the East Canyons were sitting within range of a strong charter push out of Montauk and the Rhode Island ports, and that's exactly what's playing out. Boats out of Galilee and Block Island running to Veatch are covering the same warm-water push we found at Atlantis, just from a different angle and a slightly shorter number on the plotter depending on which slice of the canyon they're working.

White marlin sign is starting to show along these same edges — a few boats working the temp breaks near Veatch have reported tailing fish and free-jumpers around the weed lines, which tracks with what we've been watching build through the month. Nothing to plan a dedicated billfish trip around just yet, but if you're already trolling the edge for tuna, it's worth dropping a spreader bar or two into the spread rather than running a straight cedar-plug program.

The honest part of this report: it's still a long day or a longer overnight, and the fish don't owe you anything for making the run. We had two good bluefin and a wahoo bite we didn't close out — that's a solid trip for late July, not a banner one. Bring enough fuel to fish the whole window and get home with a real reserve, not a guess.

Looking ahead, the first-quarter neap settling in over the next couple days should soften the current across these shelf breaks a bit, which typically widens the productive trolling window rather than concentrating it into a short tide-driven burst. If the high pressure holds through the weekend — and right now there's no reason to think it won't — I'd run to the same warm-water seam we found at Atlantis and expect the yellowfin and bigeye numbers at Veatch and Hydrographer to keep building rather than fade. Watch the eddy charts before you commit a full tank to one canyon; the warm water's been stable, but it still moves.
